B. Shift left, because a future rise always reduces current demand.
C. Stay unchanged until the future price actually changes.
D. Shift by the same amount as supply, so price cannot change today.
questions.explanation: Expected future price is a demand determinant. If buyers think tickets will cost more later, some buy now, so current demand shifts right. You do not wait for the future price to appear on today’s axis. Supply need not shift with it.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: At the current price, quantity demanded is 80 and quantity supplied is 50. There is:
options: A. A surplus of 30, and the price will tend to fall.
B. A shortage of 30, and the price will tend to rise if the market is free to adjust.
C. Equilibrium, because 80 and 50 are both positive.
D. A shortage of 130.
questions.explanation: Shortage equals quantity demanded minus quantity supplied when demand exceeds supply: 80 − 50 = 30. Unsatisfied buyers bid the price up. A surplus would require supply greater than demand. Adding the two quantities does not measure the gap.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: Price rises from $10 to $12 and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80. Using the original-price formula, |PED| is:
questions.explanation: Percentage change in quantity is 20/100 = 20%. Percentage change in price is 2/10 = 20%. |PED| = 20/20 = 1, unit elastic on this original-base calculation. 0.5 would invert the ratio. 20 confuses a percentage with the elasticity itself.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: A student reports PED as −1.5 and concludes demand is inelastic. The conclusion is:
options: A. Wrong. Elasticity is judged by the absolute value, and 1.5 is elastic.
B. Right, because any negative number is inelastic.
C. Right, because elastic demand must be positive.
D. Wrong, because a negative PED means supply, not demand.
questions.explanation: The law of demand makes PED negative. Classification uses |PED|. |−1.5| = 1.5 > 1, so demand is elastic. The sign records direction, not the elastic/inelastic label.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: A per-unit tax is placed on sellers. Demand is perfectly inelastic and supply is upward sloping. Who bears the tax?
options: A. Sellers bear the full tax.
B. The tax is shared equally.
C. Neither side bears it because the price cannot change.
D. Buyers bear the full tax.
questions.explanation: When demand is vertical, buyers do not reduce quantity as price rises, so the price paid by buyers rises by the full tax. The more inelastic side bears more of a tax. Equal sharing is not a rule; it depends on the two elasticities.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: Income rises by 10% and quantity demanded of a good rises by 4%. Income elasticity is:
options: A. 2.5, so the good is inferior.
B. 0.4, so the good is normal and income-inelastic.
C. −0.4, so the good is inferior.
D. 4, because the quantities are 4 and 10.
questions.explanation: YED = %ΔQ / %ΔY = 4/10 = 0.4. Positive YED means normal. Below 1 means income-inelastic: demand rises less than proportionally with income. Inverting the ratio or forcing a minus sign changes the good’s type.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: Why is price elasticity of supply usually lower in a short period than in a long period?
options: A. Some inputs are fixed in the short run, so output cannot change as freely.
B. The law of demand is stronger in the short run.
C. Firms always face perfectly elastic demand in the long run.
D. Supply elasticity is calculated from income, which changes slowly.
questions.explanation: PES measures how quantity supplied responds to price. With fixed plant or contracts, firms cannot expand much at once, so short-run PES is lower. This is not the law of demand, and it is not an income elasticity.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: Along a straight-line downward-sloping demand curve, PED:
options: A. Is the same number at every point because the slope is constant.
B. Falls in absolute value as you move down the curve, from elastic to inelastic.
C. Rises as you move down the curve.
D. Is zero at the midpoint.
questions.explanation: Slope is constant on a straight line, but PED uses percentage changes. High on the curve, price is high and quantity is low, so |PED| is large. At the midpoint |PED| = 1, not 0. Lower down, |PED| is less than 1.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: An effective price ceiling is set below the equilibrium price. The immediate result is:
options: A. A surplus of the good.
B. No change, because ceilings are always above equilibrium.
C. A shortage: quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the ceiling.
D. A higher quantity traded than at equilibrium.
questions.explanation: A ceiling only binds if it is below equilibrium. At that lower price, buyers want more and sellers offer less, so there is a shortage. The quantity traded is the smaller quantity supplied, which is less than the equilibrium quantity.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: An effective price floor is set above equilibrium. Which statement matches the diagram?
options: A. Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, so there is a surplus.
B. Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
C. The floor lowers the price actually paid.
D. The demand curve shifts right by law.
questions.explanation: A floor above equilibrium keeps the price high. Sellers offer more than buyers take, which is a surplus. The floor does not shift demand; it stops the price from falling to equilibrium.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: The government pays sellers a per-unit subsidy. The supply curve that buyers see will:
options: A. Shift up by the subsidy.
B. Stay still while demand shifts down.
C. Become perfectly inelastic.
D. Shift down (right) by the amount of the subsidy.
questions.explanation: A per-unit subsidy lowers sellers’ net cost, so they accept a lower price from buyers. The supply curve shifts down, or right, by the subsidy per unit. Demand does not have to move for the subsidy to change equilibrium.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: A binding quota sets the maximum quantity below the equilibrium quantity. Compared with the free market, the price tends to be:
options: A. Lower, because fewer goods always mean a lower price.
B. Higher, because the restricted quantity meets demand further up the demand curve.
C. Unchanged, because a quota is not a price control.
D. Zero, because trade above the quota is illegal.
questions.explanation: The quota caps quantity. Buyers’ willingness to pay at that smaller quantity is read off the demand curve, and it is higher than the old equilibrium price. A quota is not itself a price tag, but it changes the price that clears the allowed quantity.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: A per-unit tax creates a wedge. The deadweight loss is the:
options: A. Loss of total surplus on units that are no longer traded but were worth more to buyers than they cost sellers.
B. The whole tax revenue collected by the government.
C. The rise in producer surplus.
D. The area of consumer surplus that still remains.
questions.explanation: Tax revenue is a transfer from buyers and sellers to the government, not a loss by itself. Deadweight loss is the surplus destroyed because some mutually beneficial units are not traded. Remaining consumer surplus is a gain that still exists, not the loss.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: A price ceiling is set above the equilibrium price. Relative to the free market, the ceiling:
options: A. Creates a shortage.
B. Does not bind, so price and quantity stay at equilibrium.
C. Creates a surplus.
D. Shifts demand left.
questions.explanation: A ceiling forbids prices above it. If equilibrium is already below the ceiling, the market price is legal and nothing changes. Shortage appears only when the ceiling is below equilibrium.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: A firm’s fixed cost rises, with variable cost unchanged. In the short run, which curve shifts up?
options: A. Marginal cost only.
B. Average variable cost and marginal cost.
C. Average total cost, but not marginal cost.
D. Neither average total cost nor marginal cost.
questions.explanation: Fixed cost does not change when one more unit is produced, so marginal cost is unchanged. Average total cost includes fixed cost per unit, so ATC shifts up. AVC excludes fixed cost, so it stays put.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: Marginal cost cuts the average variable cost curve at AVC’s:
options: A. Minimum point.
B. Maximum point.
C. Starting point on the vertical axis.
D. Intersection with the demand curve.
questions.explanation: When MC is below AVC, producing one more unit pulls the average down. When MC is above AVC, it pulls the average up. So MC crosses AVC at the bottom of the U. This is a cost-curve fact, not a demand intersection.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: The law of diminishing marginal returns starts to apply when:
options: A. All inputs are varied together in the long run.
B. Total product becomes zero.
C. The firm becomes a monopoly.
D. Adding more of a variable input, with at least one input fixed, eventually lowers marginal product.
questions.explanation: Diminishing marginal returns is a short-run idea: some input is fixed. After a point, extra units of the variable input add less and less output. It is not a statement about market structure, and total product can still rise while marginal product falls.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: A bakery owner pays herself no wage and uses a shop she could have rented out for $20,000 a month. Economic cost, compared with accounting cost:
options: A. Is lower, because implicit costs are subtracted.
B. Is higher, because it includes the forgone wage and the forgone rent.
C. Is the same, because no cash is paid.
D. Ignores the $20,000 because rent was not charged.
questions.explanation: Accounting cost records explicit payments. Economic cost also includes implicit opportunity cost: the wage she could earn elsewhere and the rent she gives up. Those do not appear as cash outflows, but they are real costs of using the resources in the bakery.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: Economies of scale mean that, as the firm’s scale increases in the long run:
options: A. Long-run average cost falls.
B. Short-run marginal cost must rise at once.
C. The firm’s demand becomes perfectly inelastic.
D. Fixed cost disappears from every short-run calculation.
questions.explanation: Economies of scale are a long-run average-cost concept: a larger scale has a lower cost per unit. They are not the same as diminishing marginal returns, which is short run. Demand elasticity is a market fact, not the definition.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: A firm is making a positive accounting profit but a negative economic profit. A correct reading is:
options: A. The firm should ignore the result because only accounting profit matters in economics.
B. The firm covers its cash costs but earns less than its next-best use of resources.
C. Total revenue is below explicit cost.
D. Marginal cost is below average variable cost, so the firm must shut down at once.
questions.explanation: Negative economic profit means total revenue does not cover explicit plus implicit costs. Accounting profit can still be positive. Shutdown in the short run depends on whether revenue covers variable cost, which this comparison does not tell you.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: A price-taking firm in perfect competition faces a demand curve for its own output that is:
options: A. The market demand curve.
B. Downward sloping and equal to marginal revenue only at the midpoint.
C. Perfectly elastic at the market price.
D. Vertical, because the firm must sell a fixed quantity.
questions.explanation: The market demand can slope down, but one firm is too small to affect price. Its own demand is a horizontal line at the market price, so P = MR = AR. It is not forced to a fixed quantity.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: A single-price monopoly maximises profit where:
options: A. Marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and price is read off the demand curve above that quantity.
B. Price equals marginal cost.
C. Average revenue is minimised.
D. Marginal cost equals zero.
questions.explanation: The output rule is MR = MC for any firm that can choose quantity. A single-price monopolist then charges the price on the demand curve at that quantity, which is above MR. P = MC is the efficient benchmark, not the monopoly’s profit rule.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: Why is marginal revenue below price for a single-price monopolist?
options: A. Marginal cost is always below average cost.
B. The firm is a price taker.
C. Buyers pay different prices for the same unit.
D. To sell one more unit the firm must cut the price on all units, not only on the extra unit.
questions.explanation: A single price applies to every unit. The extra unit brings in its price, but the price cut on the previous units is lost revenue. That loss pulls MR below price. Price discrimination, where buyers pay different prices, is a different model.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: Which feature best separates monopolistic competition from perfect competition?
options: A. There is only one firm.
B. Products are differentiated, so each firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve.
C. Entry is blocked forever.
D. Firms do not maximise profit.
questions.explanation: Both structures can have free entry. Monopolistic competition has many firms and differentiated products, so demand for one firm slopes down. A single firm would be monopoly. Profit maximisation is still the usual assumption.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: In the long-run equilibrium of perfect competition, with free entry, a firm typically:
options: A. Makes zero economic profit and produces where P = minimum ATC.
B. Makes positive economic profit forever.
C. Produces where P is above ATC.
D. Shuts down because price equals marginal cost.
questions.explanation: Free entry competes economic profit away. The horizontal demand just touches ATC at its minimum, so P = MC = minimum ATC and economic profit is zero. That is not a shutdown: the firm covers all costs, including opportunity cost. Accounting profit can still be positive.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: A high barrier to entry is most important for explaining why:
options: A. A perfectly competitive firm faces a horizontal demand curve.
B. A monopoly can keep earning economic profit in the long run.
C. Marginal cost slopes upward.
D. Consumers prefer lower prices.
questions.explanation: Without a barrier, profit attracts entry and the demand facing the incumbent shrinks. A barrier stops that entry, so long-run economic profit can remain. The competitive firm’s horizontal demand comes from being a price taker, not from a barrier.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: GDP measures:
options: A. The total money held by households.
B. The value of all intermediate goods added on top of final goods, with no adjustment.
C. The market value of final goods and services produced within a country in a period.
D. Only goods sold abroad.
questions.explanation: GDP is a production measure for a territory and a time period, using market values of final output so that intermediate goods are not counted twice. Money balances are a stock of wealth, not this period’s production. Exports are only one component.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: Nominal GDP rises 8% and the price level rises 5%. A fair first reading is that:
options: A. Real output rose, but by less than 8%, because part of the rise is prices.
B. Real output rose by 8%.
C. Real output fell by 5%.
D. Nominal GDP does not include prices, so real GDP also rose 8%.
questions.explanation: Nominal GDP values output at current prices, so it mixes quantities and prices. If prices rise 5% while nominal GDP rises 8%, real GDP rises by roughly the difference, not by the full 8% and not by a fall of 5%.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: Which payment is excluded from GDP because it is a transfer, not production?
options: A. A teacher’s salary at a public school.
B. A household’s purchase of a newly built flat.
C. A firm’s purchase of a new delivery van.
D. A government cash allowance to an elderly resident, with no good or service provided in return.
questions.explanation: Transfers move income without new production. A teacher’s salary pays for a service and is in government consumption. A new flat and a new van are investment in newly produced goods. The allowance is not payment for output.
questions.subject: econ
questions.syllabus_ref: HKDSE Economics — original drill, not an HKEAA paper

questions.question: GDP and GNP differ because GNP:
options: A. Is always smaller than GDP.
B. Adds net income from abroad and is about ownership, while GDP is about location.
C. Excludes exports.
D. Measures only the price level.
questions.explanation: GDP counts production inside the territory, whoever owns the factor. GNP (or GNI) adjusts for net factor income from abroad, so it follows residents’ income. It is not a price index and it still includes trade in the underlying production accounts.

questions.question: In the expenditure approach, which list is the standard identity?
options: A. Consumption + investment + government spending + exports − imports.
B. Wages + rent + interest + profit only.
C. Consumption + imports + taxes.
D. Money supply + government spending.
questions.explanation: The expenditure identity is C + I + G + X − M. Imports are subtracted because they are in C, I or G but were not produced at home. The income approach uses factor incomes; that is a different way of measuring the same production, not a substitute list of expenditures. Money supply is not an expenditure component.

questions.question: A rise in real GDP does not, by itself, show that:
options: A. Measured market production has increased.
B. Every resident is better off, or that unpaid housework and pollution have been counted.
C. Quantities, not only prices, are part of the comparison if the deflator was used properly.
D. The figure refers to a period of production.
questions.explanation: Real GDP can rise while the gain is uneven, and it omits non-market work and many environmental costs. It does measure market production over a period, and a proper deflator removes the pure price change. Those limits are why GDP is not a complete welfare score.
